title: [Netflix] Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves outThe timeline of an investigationSo how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hoursIn our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.The disagreement underneathThe instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.The OntologyThis agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application .api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" .api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident .INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway .INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" .In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:Creating determinism from non-determinismBuilding this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:category IN sentiment IN # Result — a deterministic triple:thread:123 slack:category "incident" .thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:The five layers to create determinism from non-determinismEnrichers: Agents as entropy reducersWe use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:every entity carries an rdf:type,every URI follows a single naming scheme, andthe catalog gates every ops:Application.Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chainsThe correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute
summary: By Dhruv PratapIntroductionOrganizations that have been around for a while usually run two identity systems side by side. One belongs to the cloud provider: IAM roles, instance profiles, execution roles. The other is your own, and it is the one your internal services actually check when they decide whether to answer a request.On infrastructure you build yourself, you can bootstrap your own identity however you like. On managed compute you cannot. The provider hands your process a cloud identity and nothing else.This post describes how we close that gap for Apache Spark workloads running on Amazon EMR. A workload that starts with only an AWS identity has to end up holding a first-class internal identity. Doing the exchange is straightforward. Making it trustworthy is the part that took the design work. Very little of what follows is specific to Spark or to EMR.Two identity systemsInternal service-to-service authentication at Netflix runs on a private PKI called Metatron. Every workload gets a short-lived X.509 certificate, and services authenticate each other with mutual TLS. A workload cannot simply ask for a certificate. It is issued only after the identity service has satisfied itself that the requester really is the workload it claims to be. That verification step is called attestation. In each environment we support (VMs, containers, functions) attestation rests on some environment-specific proof that the platform can check on its own.The second concept is the Data Project, which is our unit of ownership for data. A Data Project owns tables, has a set of authorized users, and has an identity of its own. Jobs run as the Data Project rather than as the person who launched them. That is what keeps table-level access control and audit consistent across scheduled and interactive use.So the problem is this. A Spark job on managed compute starts with an AWS execution role and no internal identity. Everything it needs from inside the company (reading an encrypted column, evaluating table ACLs, holding an interactive session open longer than a short-lived token lasts) requires the internal one.One identity, one roleThe design rests on a decision made outside the Spark stack entirely. Each Data Project identity maps 1:1 to a dedicated IAM role, and the service that owns Data Project metadata records that mapping.The mapping is what makes translation possible. It lets a statement in the provider’s vocabulary (“this process is running as role R”) become a statement in ours (“this process is workload W”). Without it there is nothing to translate into, and no amount of cryptography helps. The hard part of bridging two identity systems is rarely the protocol. It is committing to a mapping and then keeping it authoritative.One practical objection arrives immediately. A single AWS account cannot hold tens of thousands of IAM roles, and we expect data projects in the order of ten thousands. We handled this by sharding data project roles deterministically across a small pool of dedicated accounts, which scales well past the projected number of projects and has the useful side effect of keeping workload roles on the far side of an account boundary from the control planes that launch them.ComponentsFive components take part.The control plane is the only service allowed to launch Spark jobs. It resolves the Data Project’s IAM role, builds and signs a workload metadata payload, and submits the job with that role as the execution role. It holds a signing key issued to it for this purpose alone.The Data Project service is the authority for the identity-to-role mapping.The Identity service receives attestation requests, verifies them, and issues certificates.A Spark plugin provides the hook. Spark 3.0+ added a plugin interface with driver-side and executor-side components that are initialized while those processes are bootstrapping.AWS STS acts as a notary, which is not its usual job.Step one: the control plane makes a signed claimWhen a job is submitted, the control plane validates the caller, looks up the Data Project’s IAM role, and builds a small payload describing the workload it is about to launch. The payload names the application identity, the mapped role, and the environment, stack and detail that the resulting credentials should be scoped to. The control plane signs the payload and passes it and the signature through as ordinary job configuration.Two properties of this step matter. First, only one service can produce a valid signature, so the set of things that can assert “this workload is legitimate” is small and auditable. Second, the payload is a claim rather than an authority. On its own it proves nothing, because job configuration travels through infrastructure we do not fully control and anything that can read it can replay it.Step two: the workload proves it holds the cloud identityWhen the managed service launches the driver process, it does so under an OS user that has the execution role’s credentials available. The driver-side plugin initializes and uses those credentials to sign, but not send, a request to the provider’s identity endpoint (sts:GetCallerIdentity). The result is a short-lived pre-signed URL.That URL is a transferable proof of possession. Anyone can fetch it. Only the holder of the role’s credentials could have produced it. And the response comes from AWS rather than from the workload, stating which role signed the request. The workload cannot lie about the answer because the workload does not supply the answer.The pattern is not new. It is the same idea behind AWS IAM authentication in HashiCorp Vault and in AWS’s own function attestation flows. It generalizes well: any environment that gives a process cloud credentials and nothing else can still produce a verifiable statement about its own identity.The plugin sends one attestation request carrying both artifacts, the pre-signed URL and the signed metadata.Step three: corroborationThe identity service does four things.It fetches the pre-signed URL against AWS STS and reads back the role that signed it. This is the provider’s statement.It verifies the metadata signature against the key issued to the control plane. This is the platform’s statement.It corroborates the two. The role AWS reports must be the role the control plane said it dispatched, for the identity the metadata names.It issues certificates for that identity, scoped to the environment, stack and detail from the signed metadata.Step 3 is the point of the whole design. Neither statement is sufficient by itself, and they fail in complementary ways. The provider’s statement is unforgeable but under-specified: it gives you a role, and a role is not a workload. It says nothing about why this process exists or what it should be allowed to be. The platform’s statement is well-specified but unverifiable on its own, for the reasons above. Put together, the signature says the workload was legitimately dispatched and the pre-signed URL says this really is it. Neither party has to trust the workload’s own account of itself.There is a tension here that we settled deliberately, and other teams should expect to meet it. The provider’s answer identifies a role, not an application. Deriving an application name from a role name is fragile string matching, and the session identifiers the platform assigns are not under our control. We chose to take the application identity from the signed metadata and use the provider’s answer only for corroboration. That costs a network round trip and a stricter signing requirement, and it buys a much clearer trust story.The fan-out problemA Spark application is one driver and up to thousands of executors, created and destroyed throughout the life of a job. Attestation designed around one process per host does not survive that.There are two defensible answers.In the first, each executor attests independently. This is uniform, adds no new trust boundary, and grounds every process’s identity in the same provider-verified proof. The cost is amplification. One large job can produce thousands of STS calls and thousands of attestation requests in a burst, which looks a lot like an attack and creates a hard dependency on provider-side rate limits.In the second, executors inherit credentials from the driver. The driver attests once and distributes credentials to executors over Spark’s internal RPC, which we configure with authentication and AES-GCM encryption so that only processes in the same application can take part. Load on the identity service stays constant. The cost is a second trust boundary and a driver that is now a credential distribution point.Considering our scale at Netflix here we went with the second approach. The general lesson is that identity amplification is a capacity question, and it is better to answer it on purpose than to have it answered for you during an incident.LifecycleCertificates are short-lived by design, so bootstrapping is only half the work. On self-managed hosts a system service handles renewal. Inside managed compute there is no equivalent hook, so the driver JVM runs a timer that re-attests on a fixed interval, well ahead of expiry. Credential material is written to a temporary directory readable only by the process owner and removed when the process exits.Executors do not refresh. They are usually short-lived, and an executor that somehow outlives its credentials can exit and be replaced, which is cheaper than making every executor a renewal client.The rule worth carrying into any similar system is that attestation has to be a repeatable operation rather than a bootstrap step. Anything that can only happen once at process start will eventually be the reason a long-running job dies nine hours in.Why this generalizesIf you run your own identity system and are moving workloads onto managed compute, the specific services here matter less than the shape of the solution.Anchor on one exchangeable primitive. A single authoritative 1:1 mapping between your identity and a provider identity is what makes translation possible. The rest is plumbing.Require two independent claims and corroborate them. One from the provider, unforgeable and under-specified. One from your control plane, well-specified and replayable. Trust the intersection and never either alone.Keep the signer scarce. If exactly one service can make the platform’s claim, your trust story fits in a sentence.Hook the layer you still own. On managed compute you rarely control the host or its init system, but you almost always control the runtime: a plugin, an agent, an entrypoint. Attestation belongs there.Decide the amplification policy on purpose. Distributed engines multiply every per-process operation by their parallelism.Make attestation repeatable and credentials short-lived. Renewal is a requirement, not a follow-up.What makes the result trustworthy is that no single participant issues an identity by itself. Not the workload, not the control plane, not the provider. And the workload, which is the party in the weakest position to be trusted, is never asked to vouch for itself.AcknowledgementsThanks to Amer Hesson for the Data Project abstraction, Nick Siow for the Data Project IAM role sharding, and Doug Clark for Metatron attestation.Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
summary: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen MareddyStratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1resources: numCpus: 8 memoryInMB: 18000 diskSizeInMB: 50000 networkInMbps: 1000Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.The Challenge: Over-ProvisioningWhen engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.Meet the Stratum Resource TunerTo address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:Figure 1: SRT Workflow High-LevelCollect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).Verify the recommendation through experiments.Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:Figure 2: Recommendation State MachineCREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.Metrics CollectionTo make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:Figure 3: Metrics CollectionExecution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:{ "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a", "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "tags.stratum.phase": "run", "tags.stratum.success": true, "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26, "tags.cpuCount": 8, "tags.memoryInMB": 18000, "tags.diskInMB": 50000, "tags.networkInMbps": 1000, "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1", "ts": 1780743028000}In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:{ "span_id": "38536313f65f060a", "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "phase": "run", "success": true, "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002, "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028, "runtime_secs": 26, "cpu_requested": 8, "memory_mb_requested": 18000, "disk_mb_requested": 50000, "network_mbps_requested": 1000, "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "env": "prod", "resource_usage": }Recommendation GenerationA scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.Figure 4: Recommendation Generation SequenceFor each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:CPU recommendation{ "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU", "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4, "status": populates the remaining parameters.When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.Retry with More ResourcesWe take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.Figure 5: Retry with More ResourcesThis “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.Recommendation VerificationEvery recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.Figure 6: Evaluating StageSynthetic experiment:Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.Typically runs for 1–2 hours.Runs to completion without early termination checks.Figure 7: Synthetic Experiment FlowProduction experiment:Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.Figure 8: Production Experiment FlowThe Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:{ "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7", "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 }, "productionExperiment": { "enabled": true, "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating }}Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:{ "outcome": "APPLIED", "syntheticExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }, "productionExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }}The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.Post-Apply MonitoringPassing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.Figure 9: Unexpected Retries SpikeBecause early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.Figure 10: Recommendation Auto-RevertWe intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.Where Are We TodayOversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.Looking ahead, our key priorities include:Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.CreditsSpecial thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Engineering at Meta] Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
summary: Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for. GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers. GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas: 1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun, co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results. 2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM, a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation (Solaris) to harvest the gains from the upstream model. 3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously. Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and across every key advertiser objective from off-site conversions to mobile app installs. The generalizable representations learned on data-rich click tasks transfer into data-sparse conversion tasks. A new training recipe with cost-free data mixing and the domain expert framework makes this heterogeneous, large-scale learning tractable, with predictable scale and enhanced reliability. 4. Scaling Total Training FLOPs by 4x While Doubling E2E Training Efficiency Across Thousands of GPUs Challenge: Training a RecSys foundation model across thousands of GPUs at this scale requires careful orchestration of compute, parallelism, communication, and memory. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization while scale. Solution: We developed custom kernels with low precision and new 5D parallelism strategies co-designed with the latest GPU hardware and Meta’s training cluster, and optimized model architecture with infrastructure together to scale efficiently across thousands of GPUs. End-to-end training efficiency is doubled to 20-25% model FLOPS utilization (MFU) with 4x total training FLOPs, enabling GEM to train at LLM-scale at Meta (see full technical story in our companion blog on Training GEM at LLM Scale). Scaling Law: Bend Scaling Curve at Frontier Scale with Kunlun GEM introduces a new LLM-style model architecture — Kunlun. Compared to the previous version (Interformer), Kunlun delivers 2x performance gains with the same computation scaling. Kunlun is designed around the following innovations: Standardize and unify architecture framework by seamlessly interleaving lifelong sequence modeling with scalable recommendation-specific cross-interaction. Introduce scalable architecture through deep co-design with the latest generation of hardware, and computation reduction with almost no model quality regression. Innovate efficient sequence scaling to process longer user engagement contexts with offline sequence infrastructure. The scaling law pattern on the light-weight model of GEM with small parameter size. Efficient Architecture for Scaling Recommendations GEM’s Kunlun architecture effectively bends the recommender system scaling curve at frontier training scales by empowering ultra-long user sequences and massive user-item interaction features. For the following technical discussion, we define two types of features: non-sequence features (such as user demographics, ad content representations), and sequence features with a sequence of events, each composed of a set of features. This architecture introduces three fundamental advancements: 1. A Standardized and Unified Architecture Framework We advanced the LLM-style architecture to better capture the unique characteristics of recommender system models — specifically, heterogeneous features and data dynamics. Each layer consists of: Attention: customize the attention and feed-forward networks to capture the long dependency pattern in user behavior by adapting to data dynamics. Summarization Component: simplify and enhance the summarization architecture to extract critical user insights from sequences, effectively bridging sequence and non-sequence structure. Cross Interaction: expand to the mixture-of-experts (MoE) style design, enabling large-scale modeling of complex interactions between sequence and non-sequence features. 2. Introducing Scalable Architecture Through Deep Co-design We co-designed the architecture with the latest generation of hardware to allow it to grow deeper and wider efficiently: Computation Complexity Reduction via Block Attention: Replacing full self-attention with block-aligned sparse attention reduces the complexity associated with sequence length from quadratic to linear relative to window size, and uses only the window size that is a multiple of block size, friendly for the kernel without partial block size. Component Unification via Architecture Reformulation: Per-Example Feed-Forward Networks (pFFN) was introduced to adapt the traditional FFN to per-example distribution. We reformulated the pFFN component into attention operations through Generalized Dot-Product Attention (GDPA), speeding up training by targeting at unifying the model’s many attention-like operations into a single GPU kernel, delivering up to 2x forward speedup. Scalable Cross interaction through Expert Parallelism: Our cross-interaction component utilizes a scalable, MoE-like framework that employs model-expert parallelism, allowing each GPU to process a subset of expert sub-networks in parallel. 3. Innovating Efficient Sequence Scaling We introduced specialized component designs to make ultra-long sequences computationally tractable: Component Skip Connection (CompSkip): The computational skip mechanism selectively activates sequence modules in each layer, and only routes outputs through residual connections. By selectively deactivating the specific components, which is based on the assumption that the network can recover quickly after re-activating, we reduce FLOPS by 43% with negligible quality loss. Sequence Unification (OneSeq): We selectively unify user sequences chronologically after the event feature aggregation. This allows a single, unified sequence layer to process long sequences, even when individual events possess heterogeneous structures and features. In the system, we have different user sequence sources, some of which have different events features. For example, an event in a purchase sequence can be described by ad ID and account ID, while the event in a post sequence is described by actors and object ID. They cannot simply be unified from the data source level due to the different set of event features. It requires the flexible sequence unification approach to maximize GPU efficiency because of large-size tensor operations and minimizing operator fragmentation. The GEM Architecture. On the left is the building block, and right is an illustration of the computation skip mechanism. How Ultra-Long Sequences Matter The new architecture makes ultra-long sequences feasible. GEM scaled the long engagement context length by 2x in production, and further enabled the capability of scaling long context to 25x, demonstrating infrastructure capability at frontier scale. Along the way, we discovered: Prediction quality follows a power law with sequence length. The relationship is predictable and consistent across sequence lengths. Larger models benefit disproportionately from longer sequences. This creates a virtuous cycle: scaling compute makes the model bigger, which makes longer sequences more valuable. Scaling sequence length makes the model more accurate, which justifies more compute. The two scaling laws reinforce each other, offering investment directions to bend the overall scaling law curve beyond simply adding compute. Post-Training: Knowledge Transfer at Scale The value of the foundation model depends on how effectively its intelligence transfers to the hundreds of vertical models that serve ads in real time. GEM revolutionizes post training for recommendation systems through the structure representation with the deep historical memory from the central brain, achieving 2x of transfer effectiveness beyond knowledge distillation. Furthermore, async computation is introduced to a few domain-specific foundation models to transfer the knowledge to vertical models. Structure Representation at Scale Knowledge distillation is effective but limited in bandwidth: downstream models only receive a compressed view of GEM’s intelligence at each training process. To address the limitation, we introduce the precomputed structure representation, such as LoopFM, to understand and compress the central brain from the foundation model into a compact representation, and then structure it with deep historical memory. It enables the downstream models to learn the long context from our central brain. It consists of the following major components across the system: Understand and Compress Intelligence: We compress the intelligence from GEM into the compact representations, which are summarized from the important layers, and used to comprehensively describe the event (or data) that is processed by the foundation model. Structure with Deep Historical Memory: We structure its compact representation together with the representations that the foundation model previously generated for the same user into a sequential context window, capturing user intent dynamics across all surfaces and traffic through GEM’s memory. Learn from Long Context Intelligence: Downstream models will learn the structure representation with long historical context through the specialized architecture during both inference and training time. The representation generation process is precomputed and shared with the computation to generate soft labels of the foundation model for knowledge distillation without additional foundation model cost. The structure representation paradigm. Speculative Precomputation for Fresh Predictions Solaris keeps knowledge transfer fresher, precomputing the user-ad representation from GEM just before vertical model inference needs it. Evaluating the large-scale model inside a live ad request is not affordable, Solaris moves it in time: It speculatively precomputes foundation model embeddings for the user-ad pairs a future request is likely to need, and delivers them just-in-time on the serving hot path. Downstream models gain access to near-real-time foundation model intelligence without being constrained by the latency. Borrowing the idea of speculative decoding from LLM serving, Solaris works through the following major components across the system: Deliver Fresh Runtime Knowledge: It generates the user-ad embedding directly, giving vertical models real-time, point-to-point knowledge of how a specific user is likely to act on the exact ad candidate. Speculate Ahead of the Request: As multi-stage ranking narrows a live request down to its top ad candidates, Solaris evaluates those user-ad pairs with the foundation model in asynchronous background jobs. The computation carries no latency budget with elastic capacity while it can capture rich knowledge. Enrich Coverage Hierarchically: When an exact user-ad embedding is unavailable, the system degrades rather than drops. It substitutes an aggregate of the user’s own recent embeddings across the same ad groups, or borrows from behaviorally similar users. Solaris speculative precomputation. Large-Scale Cross-Domain Optimization: Optimize Across Surfaces and Funnels We further trained GEM with the ads data at Meta scale, including all-surface data (e.g., Facebook and Instagram Feed and Reels/video) and deep funnel optimization (e.g., off-site conversion, mobile app install). GEM powers the first optimized model that jointly predicts both CTR across all the surfaces and conversion rate (CVR) across the major optimization goals. Previously, each surface and each prediction objective had its own system. This means learnings from engagement patterns across platforms can more directly be used to understand its conversion behavior (e.g., purchase) across ad surfaces. This positions GEM as the central model and compute engine for ads recommendation across Meta’s advertising surfaces. Unlike LLMs with the static data, RecSys models need to deal with data dynamics and freshness as well as the diverse distribution across surfaces and traffic. To overcome the challenge, GEM built the first training recipe for the large-scale cross-surface, cross-domain unification through: A Cost-Free Data Mixing Strategy: It introduced virtual data loading from different combinations of data pipelines without physically merging data together and incurring additional storage cost. It can flexibly adapt to the current ads ecosystem where the downstream models still train with the specific surface or traffic data. We also design a data mixture mechanism to control the mixture proportions during offline and online training close to the real datastream order received in real time, mitigating instability for domain switch and overmemorization for the recent domain data. A Domain Expert Framework: A shared expert learns a unified representation across all domains, while domain-specific experts capture surface-specific patterns. Each domain expert benefits from both: the shared cross-domain knowledge and its own specialized knowledge. Experts are built on top of the Kunlun architecture framework. Training a RecSys Model at LLM-Scale Efficiently GEM now trains at LLM scale on several thousand of the latest-generation GPUs. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics and rich user & ads signal interaction patterns that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization for training a foundational recommendation model of GEM’s size. We measure training efficiency through E2E MFU, which decomposes into two factors: E2E MFU = Local MFU (compute efficiency) × Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency). Local MFU (compute efficiency) measures how well a single GPU’s compute units are utilized — how close the workload runs to the hardware roofline. Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency) measures how much single-GPU performance is retained when distributing across thousands of GPUs. This decomposition matters because it lets us treat compute efficiency and scaling efficiency as related but distinct optimization problems, each with its own dedicated set of techniques. Both must be addressed to maximize end-to-end MFU. We tackled these challenges through complementary compute efficiency and scaling efficiency innovations: Compute efficiency: Achieved through a customized recommendation kernel library — Jagged Flash Attention (JFA), GDPA, Block-Attention, etc. — and mixed ultra-low precision training (including MXFP8 attention and MLP) optimized for recommendation workloads, purpose-built to leverage the latest generation GPU architecture. Scaling efficiency: Topology-aware 5D parallelism with Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)-free collectives — 2D FSDP + Expert Parallelism for dense parameters, combined with Fully Sharded 2D Model Parallelism for sparse parameters — co-designed with Meta’s multi-tiered network hierarchy to reduce communication overhead. The result: We doubled GEM’s E2E training efficiency to 20-25% MFU over the past 12 months while scaling total training FLOPs by 4x. Training a foundation model at the intersection of LLMs and recommendation systems is a co-design problem, not a software problem or a hardware problem alone. This 2x efficiency gain came from carefully considering every layer of the stack for optimization — kernels, precision, parallelism, networking, and memory all had to move together. For the full technical story, see our companion blog: GEM Training: Train Meta’s LLM-Scale Ads Recommendation Model Efficiently. The Future of RecSys Foundation Models Looking forward, we are excited to extend GEM to learn from all of Meta’s platform data, capturing behavior across organic and ads engagements spanning text, images, and video. We’re building toward LLM-scale long context, giving the model the ability to reason over longer spans of engagement context. This will unlock better ad relevance and help advertisers connect with the right audiences more efficiently. We will continue to scale GEM on even larger compute clusters, opening new scaling opportunities. We are introducing AI-driven optimizations, such as ecosystem enhancement and architecture co-design, to accelerate future evolutions. These optimizations will iteratively refine model architecture in lockstep with hardware advancements, so that each new generation delivers more intelligence per dollar of compute. We will evolve the post-training paradigm with reasoning capability to transfer more of this intelligence to downstream models, further improving advertiser performance and user experience.
